utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Matthew Gillett, case manager Thomas Laugel, and intern Ivana Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber will now rule on the tenth Prosecution motion for leave to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list filed on 19 April. We understood that the Defence does not object. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution requests to add three photographs to its 65 ter list, the Trial Chamber grants the Prosecution leave to add these three photographs to its exhibit list. The Chamber notes that both the eighth and the tenth motion of the Prosecution stem from the documents it identified on 18 March 2013. The Chamber considers that it would be -- that it will be more efficient -- a more efficient use of everybody's time if the Prosecution were to review these documents and make a comprehensive motion for any further documents it wishes to have added to its 65 ter list. If there's nothing else, we can call the next witness. Closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Witness. Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. First of all, do you understand me in -- do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, as you have protective measures, we will not mention your name. We will refer to you either by your number -- by your witness number or just by Mr. Witness. Mr. Gillett, I take it you have a pseudonym sheet?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yes. That's 65 ter document 6412.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you please verify whether your name and date of birth on that sheet on the screen are correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I must point out to you that by doing so, you expose yourself to the penalty of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Please give the solemn declaration now. The usher will give you the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Pseudonym sheet to be admitted, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P1637, admitted under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Gillett, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning. And good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you hear me loud and clear?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for a couple of questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what was the atmosphere like in Eastern Slavonia and Vojvodina in mid to late 1991?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Movement became difficult. The last time I drove on the motorway, sometime in the middle of 1991, there was growing intolerance between various ethnic communities, that is to say, Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You said movement was difficult. Moving to November 1991, was there a time when you were stopped or arrested at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: That was the last time when I was driving from Zagreb on the motorway towards Novi Sad and suddenly a group of uniformed JNA members showed up on the road, stopped me, searched my car, asked for my documents, questioned me about where I was going. And when I was crossing into Vojvodina I was stopped again. They questioned me again in the streets of Novi Sad, and it was all about the same thing. Every other time after that when I was going towards Slavonia, I would go via Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were you arrested in Titov Vrbas?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Yes. In Titov Vrbas, I was working with a Serb colleague. I was sitting in the car while he went away to agree about the presentation of these cosmetic products when two men in civilian clothing approached the car, dragged me out of the car, and they treated me rather rudely and roughly. They waited for my colleague to show up and then they took us both to the police station, to the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And in what country is Titov Vrbas located?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: That's Vojvodina, perhaps 50 kilometres from Novi Sad where I was living at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: When they arrested you in Titov Vrbas, did they provide any reason or do you know why they arrested you?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Well, they did not tell me the reason, but already at that time the Borovo Naselje incident had happened and they probably reacted to my licence plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: What was it about your licence plates that they would have reacted to?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: The licence plates were Virovitica, a place in Croatia. I was in Vojvodina, though, and there were many similar licence plates in Vojvodina too at the time. Probably because people were moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You said they took you to the police station in Titov Vrbas. What did they do there?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: They separated my colleague and myself. We spent about four or five hours there. They began questioning us. Why I was there, what I was doing, et cetera. One of them wanted to be rough with me, but they stopped him. And then they continued questioning me to see who I am, why I was there, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did they take you anywhere after being in the Titov Vrbas police station?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: They put the two of us into a police car. Two men sat in front, one of them held us at gunpoint all the time, and the car was driven by uniformed policemen. We went together towards Novi Sad where they brought me to the provincial SUP, the one that covers probably the entire region. It was a police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what happened at the provincial SUP?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: They continued to question me. I learned later that my colleague was released. I was kept there. And around 2.00 a.m., when the policemen and interrogators rotated, they tried to get out of me as much information as they could using the good cop/bad cop routine, but they were obviously not happy that I couldn't tell them because I didn't know what they asked. Then they brought me to Novi Sad late at night and told me to come back in the morning. They had kept my car, all the samples that I kept in my car, et cetera. So later I returned to the same place and interrogation resumed until 2.00 or 3.00 a.m. They were rougher and rougher all the time, although they didn't beat me. They threatened to take me to the front line to defend Serbian houses. And then around 2.00 or 3.00 a.m., they drove me away in a car that had no licence plates - I remember that very well - and took me to the next point which I later learned was called Paragovo where there was a military barracks and basically turned me over to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Was there anyone else detained with you at the Paragovo military barracks?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: They took me to a facility that I suppose was a prison. There were seven or eight people there already in a room of about 10 to 12 square metres with bars on the windows. There were some kind of beds on the floor where people were lying one on top of another. And the next morning a military policeman came -- in fact, he was there all the time as a guard. In the morning they would take us out, line us up. We would stand with our heads bent down and our hands behind our back. That lasted throughout the morning. They made us sweep and clean the compound of the barracks. And then in the afternoon, they took me again for an interrogation. The people there were all in uniform, military men, there was one captain, I believe, and another officer whose rank I don't remember. Anyway, the questioning continued. They were trying to find out what I know and there was still no violence at that time. Everything

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: that's the reason because other people were beaten --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry, could I interject there and ask: Do you remember who any of the people that were detained with you were, their names or who they were?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: don't know the man's name. I remember his car was there which means he had been on his way somewhere when he was detained and he had been there quite a long time before I came. And later in the camp I recognised two or three other men including Dr. Mladen Loncar. I saw him later at the camp too. And there were a couple of reservists who had come there in uniform and I suppose they were there for trying to dodge military service. There were two or three men from Croatian places who refused to join the reserve in the military, and after this refusal or protest, they took them to that place. That's mainly what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw Mladen Loncar at the camp too. Which camp are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Later, after two or three days after interrogation, I was placed alone in a car. There was only a little tiny window facing the driver and they took me I didn't know where, but I later realised it was the Begej [phoen] camp where I met Loncar and another two or three men who had been in Paragovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And where is the Begej camp located, in what country?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: It's in the eastern part of Vojvodina near a place called Srpska Crnja, above Zrenjanin, in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Is it also -- can it be pronounced Begejci, the name of this camp?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Yes. There's a small town nearby called Begejci.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you some questions about the Begejci camp now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett, can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, when you first arrived at Begejci camp, how were you received?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I was afraid being driven in that car because I was thinking all the time about the threat that I was going to Papuk, a war zone, a front line, according to what I'd heard before. And since they were driving me I don't know where, our first stop was Novi Sad and I thought for a moment they would take me home. However, the door was opened, there were military policemen with those white belts, and they were saying, "Let's see this birdie, Ustasha, he's going to pay for it." And then they started threatening me again so obviously they were not taking me home. And through that little window facing the driver I could see some kind of woods and I started getting really worried that they would do something to me. But then I realised they were taking me to a kind of barn with a wire fence around it. Very roughly they pulled me out of that vehicle, started hitting me on the neck, saying, "Head down, hands behind your back." The man who met me there, a man in uniform, threw me against the wire fence, beating me all the time. When he threw me against the wire fence I tried to make sure I wouldn't be too badly cut, and then they dragged me towards that big barn. Two men at the entrance took me over, pulled me into the barn, and from the corner of my eye I saw it was a huge space, 30 to 40 square metres. There were people lying on the floor, covered over the head with army blankets. Again, there was a military policeman sitting at a desk and he started to interrogate me, who I was, what I was doing, how many people I had killed, what weapon I had used. All the time I was held by the other two, head down, hands behind the back. They were getting rougher and rougher, walking around me with a truncheon, and I had the impression that he would hit me with that truncheon so I cringed. He started cursing my mother and started to hit me -- to kick me in the head but he actually got me in the shoulder. The other two were already beating me, and after that was over, he ordered that I be relocated to a position where I spent the next month.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If I could just go back through a couple of the details of what you've just told us, firstly, the military policeman that you said pushed you into the wire fence, do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Later I learned that his nickname was Zare. He had a couple of nicknames. We never heard their true names, Vojo, Zare, Rambo, those were the nicknames that I heard. Borko was another. There were some seven or eight, but not more than ten people whom I saw entering the barn, or rather, that portion where we were put up. And there were also some reserves armed with rifles keeping guard, but they never entered. There was probably a sort of hierarchy in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what uniform was this individual nicknamed Zare wearing?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: He was wearing a JNA uniform and a white belt that he sometimes wore and sometimes didn't. Anyway, it was a JNA uniform. Rambo was one of them wearing a camouflage uniform. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You mentioned that you came into a big hall and that you were asked questions and physically mistreated by individuals. Do you know the names of those individuals that mistreated you inside the main hall?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: The two holding me I later learned had the same status as me, that is, they were prisoners who were some sort of go-betweens between us, the rest of the prisoners, and them, the army. They had to be by the entrance all the time, that's where they slept, but in shifts. One of them had to be awake at any point in time. Whenever one of us had to go to the toilet, we had to report to them. Or when we were taken to be interrogated, they called our names and took us to the entrance. It was Mirko from Bilje, I don't know his last name, and they called the other man Krasniqi, he must have been an Albanian. I don't know how he got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And when these two individuals were holding you, when you first entered the barn or main hall, did the military policemen tell them to stop at any occasion?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Nobody said anything. I later understood that this was the regular procedure. Any new arrivals were subjected to the main procedures -- the procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were being shouted at, mistreated, and some of them were used as dummies for practicing karate kicks and punches. They were being beaten for a couple of days and then they were interrogated like me, and it was the same with everyone. We then covered our heads with blankets so as not to have to look at that, but we couldn't avoid hearing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get 65 ter document 2415 on the monitor, please, without this being broadcast publicly and this should be tab 4. We only need the original of this. It's a diagram. And could we rotate it 90 degrees clockwise? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this diagram?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Yes. It's a sketch of the Begejci camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And who drew this sketch?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I did. I drew it from memory but I don't know when exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could get --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: If we could get some help from the usher to provide the witness with the equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'd ask you, Witness, to indicate with a 1 the location where you were thrown into the fence when you first arrived at the camp.

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And could you indicate with an arrow the direction that you came from when you arrived in the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I can draw the vehicle, this is where it stopped approximately, and they dragged me this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And Your Honours will note there are some terms written on the diagram. There is an English translation attached to some of these -- for most of these terms. I'll ask the witness that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: One of the locations referred to is a machine-gun nest. Firstly, do you see the machine-gun nest; and secondly, which direction were the machine-guns facing in the nest?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I'll mark it. And the machine-guns were pointed towards the entrance gate. There was a machine-gun pointing this way at any point in time. But there's also a wire fence. The machine-gun was outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And is the wire fence the thin line right beside the machine-gun nest?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Right in front of the machine-gun nest, some 10 metres away from the barn gate, the gate to the room in which we were lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And I'll note for the record that the machine-gun nest is marked with an X with a triangular top.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you to indicate the main barn that you've referred to with a big circle around it.

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, within the circle you've just drawn but just to the left of the rectangular building we see some lines, two more or less parallel lines with some writing. Could you explain what they are?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: This was a roofed-over spot where we ate. Food was distributed there and you could put your plastic plate there on that bar when there was such food.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could you mark with a 2 that location where you ate?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I'm going to return to this diagram subsequently with a couple more markings. So can I suggest that we MFI it for the meanwhile so that we don't end up with multiple copies of the same diagram?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gillett, we'll MFI the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P1638, MFI and under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we now get 65 ter document 6413 on the monitor and that should be tab number 5. And if we could go to page 2 of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, looking at the upper picture, if we could focus on that, can you describe what this is?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: This is the structure that I marked with the number 2, where we ate. You see it's roofed over, and between these vertical structures there were places where we could lay our plates. And you can tell that this was taken at the time when food was being distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we look at the lower picture on the same page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, these men are all lined up. What are they doing?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: This was the food line. Normally we had to bow our heads, but we weren't allowed to stand upright normally. This was just before food was distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Why did you have to bow your heads?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: We were obliged to do so since we came to Paragovo, you weren't allowed to look at anybody, only look down. One of the guards who was standing to our right, when one of us looked at him, I was warned but didn't react immediately -- the man looked at the guard and the guard ordered me to slap him on the face because of that. But I wouldn't do that and then the other man was ordered to slap me. So we had to bow our heads all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And when the man was ordered to slap you, did he, in fact, do that?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Yes, he did but he didn't slap me hard. He knew that we would both have to bear the consequences if he refused to do so. I knew too but I didn't care. I knew that our fate would be the same either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender this document 6413 for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P1639.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go back to the diagram 2415 that was MFI'd as P1638, please. And if we could go into private session for just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, the small dashes, there's a large number of them inside the main barn, what do they indicate?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: These are people lying there. I tried to indicate it that way when I drew this. When I was assigned the spot marked 3, the left wall and the right wall were already full and on the right side almost up to the gate. And the spot that I indicated with a 3 was the fourth row. There must have been about a hundred men in that hall. Day and night there was light -- actually, there were reflectors in all four corners and we spent most of the time lying there on some straw that was -- there was a concrete floor covered with a bit of straw. We got a tarpaulin and a blanket.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And I suggest if -- when -- if this is eventually admitted it is under seal. We probably don't need a redaction of the reference to the number 3 from a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, when -- while you were detained in this hall, what was the total number of -- approximate total number of detainees that were detained there during the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: When I entered the barn for the first time, I suppose there must have been some 300 people in there. Some of them had arrived a month before me. Later on some 500 or 530 in all. Once there were 500-odd people in there, then some of them had to sleep in the troughs for feeding livestock. Not sure about the exact term. I think it's called a trough where you put the feed for the livestock.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: That's correct. And where did the majority of these detainees come from?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: The eastern part of Slavonia, that is, Opatovac, Ilok, Bapska, Sotin, up until the fall of Vukovar and from this -- this spot marked 3, down to the gate all the places were taken by people from Vukovar, civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now get 65 ter document 2916.1 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What about this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'll be coming back to it so could we maintain the MFI status as P1638.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But we'll have to save it, then, with the new markings. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Witness, here we have a list of persons that are listed as being detained at the Begejci camp. In proofing, did you go through this list and mark the individuals who you recognised?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Yes, I had a look at the list and marked some people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've highlighted those markings. If you look at page 5, for example, we should see one of those come up. And through the rest of the list you'll see similar markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: In relation to the individual shown here - and I won't state his name in the interests of not identifying yourself - could you describe how he was treated when he was at Begejci?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: He was lying very close to where I was, the spot marked 3, that is. He had gone through everything that I had to go through, but I also know from other people that he hung for two days from a pole with his hands tied and he suffered consequences because probably his -- the nerves of his -- some nerves in his body were damaged. And of course he was beaten, which was the normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And you'll notice, Your Honours, on this list he's identified eight individuals, but the witness's name is not featured on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So, Mr. Witness, could I ask you why it is that there are so few out of the several hundred that you recognise and why your own name is not on this list?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I was from elsewhere. These are mostly people from some villages, they all knew each other, and those who compiled this list couldn't have known my name. But mostly everybody there belonged to groups of co-villagers or fellow townsmen from Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would seek the admission of 2916.1 and that will have to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P1640. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you mentioned a moment ago that there were -- people in the hall were civilians. What proportion of the detainees in the main hall were civilians?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: A small number of them just across from where I was wore uniforms. There were about 20 of them and they were said to belong to the ZNG from Belisce. Everyone else was civilians as far as I know. They were still wearing some parts of camouflage uniforms. According to the stories I heard, that group had been betrayed because they were headed to a position on the Hungarian border but they had been surrounded and taken to Beli Manastir where they were put in dogs' cages, and some of them were wounded allegedly by dogs who were turned at them. Later on their wounds were treated and bandaged; we saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: What ethnicity were the majority of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: There were mostly Croats. Some of them were Romanians, three or four of them. There were two black men from Sri Lanka, allegedly. They were students. There were even some Serbs. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: How were the Serbs treated?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: The same way as we were as far as I was able to observe. There weren't many of them. I remember two or three of them who were close to where I was, but they were treated the same way as we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You've mentioned that you were mistreated in various ways and other detainees were as well. So why would the Serb guards mistreat other Serbs who were detained at Begejci?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that these Serbs who found themselves there probably did not agree with the current politics, they didn't want to put on a uniform, they didn't want to go fight in other areas in Croatia or Bosnia later, and thus they were condemned to be treated the same like us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a few questions about the conditions at Begejci. First, what was the temperature like when you were there in late 1991?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: It was already cold and it was getting colder and colder as the winter went on. It was very difficult to stand because we only had the clothes in which we were arrested. In that whole month we were allowed to have a bath only once some seven days before the exchange. We could never change our clothes, our shoes, or anything. The first week out of fear and the pressure created by interrogation, for instance, unless you respond immediately when called out, you get beaten. So for the first ten days I never took my shoes off, terribly worried that something would go wrong if I do. Anyway, people wore the clothes in which they were arrested. Some even put plastic bags on their heads because of the draft. It was a very old barn. There were no conditions for normal living.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were you provided with medical care?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: As for medical assistance, a lady doctor would come two or three times to change the bandages of those uniformed detainees from the home guard and this job was taken over later by Dr. Loncar, I suppose because when they realised there was a physician among us, they didn't want to invite anyone from outside anymore. There was also a man who was a cook by occupation, so basically we did all the work ourselves. I suppose, but I can only suppose, that they wanted to bring in as few outsiders as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And did the female medical personnel or Dr. Loncar have adequate facilities to care for the injuries to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I know he had some bandages and some pills like painkillers, nothing much because there were people who were missing pieces of flesh.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Perhaps we should get a redaction just of that last reference to the sleeping location.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you have described being pushed into the wire fence when you first arrived and then being beaten in the barn on that first day upon arrival. Aside from those two instances, were you physically mistreated on any other occasions at the camp?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: After three or four nights spent in that barn when there was mistreatment every night, five or six reservists would come in, and I'll describe one case in particular when they came with those German Shepherds that were normally kept within the compound inside the wire fence. They brought those dogs inside and one dog was breathing hard right into my ear. At that moment the image in my head of those people with bite wounds and the people who were running from one side to another on their orders, trampling all over the rest of us. All the time there was some kind of torture going on. But one of the routines in the camp was that all the newcomers had to go through this torture, all of it, before they would be interrogated. Since I was alone, I was brought there as an individual, those six men in JNA uniforms took turns beating me. One had a truncheon and beat me on the left leg, probably wanting to bring me down, and I had been forewarned that if I do fall they would start kicking me. So he hit me three or four times on my upper leg and the last time he missed and hit one of his colleagues. Then I was taken over by this man called Zare who said, "Give him to me." He took off my watch, he beat me on the head, he hit me with his knee in the stomach, and until I started bleeding from the mouth he wouldn't stop beating me. When they saw I was bleeding, they stopped beating me. Of course for the next ten days I wasn't able to stand up from the pain in my stomach and generally. I had -- I needed help to stand up. And the same happened to everyone there. They would be taken out to interrogation every three or four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You mentioned in your last answer that "people were running from one side to another on their orders, trampling all over the rest of us." Could you tell us whose orders these were?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Those few men who were allowed to go into the barn, Zare, Borko, the men I've already mentioned, that one called Vojo. But Zare stands out in my memory because of all the ugly things that he did to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And in relation to those individuals you've just named, you talked about the uniforms they wore. Do you know anything else about their background?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: In the night where this was happening, and they were wont to come into the barn when they were drunk and mistreat us, one of them said he didn't care where he was - we overheard their conversation - he said he didn't care whether he was in prison, behind bars, or behind a wire fence. So I suppose those were people who had been serving a prison sentence and then they converted into reservists and continued to serve in that way. Zare had scars on his face from some prior brawls, I suppose, but these are all my assumptions. That's all I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You've mentioned interrogations. Were you, yourself, interrogated at Begejci?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: After this torture I was taken to the premises drawn in the first part. There was hay on the floor. And again they made me write statements, several pages, but they would come back in all the time and beat me, saying I had written too little. And sometimes I was called out to go to the different location where I was interrogated. The last time they called me out, they took me to the dormitory of those men I've mentioned because I saw their beds there. I found a sergeant in that room, his feet on the desk, a bottle of brandy on the desk, and there were another two or three who pushed me onto a bed. First of all, they brought in that briefcase with which I had come containing the documents of my company and other information. The briefcase had to be opened before them and they had the code, but I later realised the point was to take the money that was inside because, in the end, I didn't find the valuables and the money that had been there. There was also this thing like a Taser and the man to whom the bed belonged threatened that he would kill me because I had lain on his bed being dirty as I was. It was all very strange, but the point was obviously to open my briefcase and take what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: What types of questions did they ask you?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: The routine was always the same: How many people did you kill? What kind of weapon did you carry? You are a spy, and even if you're not a spy, you are a hardened Ustasha. And they called us other name. The point was only mistreatment and abuse because whatever answer you gave, it didn't matter. They would always find a reason to abuse us more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we're at 10.15. Is that time for the break or is it 10.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You mentioned the dormitory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get document 2415 - which is the one that's been MFI'd P1638 - on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And with the usher's assistance, if you could indicate with a number 4 the location where you were interrogated by the individual with the brandy.

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You said that there were another two or three there at the same time, do you know who they were? During that interrogation.

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: They were standing by me and hitting me. At one point that man came with a Taser and waved it in my face, but they didn't really use it. The interrogations were such that people fainted as soon as they were called out. It's hard to tell you about everybody's experience, but I know about Dr. Loncar and a blue car would come for him, and I know that he was shaking like a leaf every time he knew he had to go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And at any time did they tell you the reason for which you were detained at the Begejci camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get a redaction just of the lines of that last answer referring to the relatives. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you please inform the Registrar of what exactly you want to redact in -- with your previous question -- the previous redaction request you did, it's not quite clear what you want to have redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So for this one it's okay, but for the previous one ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Perhaps I could check that at the break? Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We need to implement it right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So you'll have to look it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sure. This was page 22, line 21, and it's the location of where he was sleeping, the person he was sleeping next to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just line --

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Just line 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- 21? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, while you were at Begejci, did anyone die?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: One man died -- perhaps I should show it on the picture. He was at the same level as I but next to the wall. We had been ordered out. He failed to get up and then they realised what had happened, and I know Dr. Loncar took him to Zrenjanin, under escort, of course. He was transferred to Zrenjanin. That's the information I have. The man succumbed to the beatings. He was an older man.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And was he a civilian or a soldier, do you know?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: A civilian surely. That entire area, only those 20 facing me were not civilians; all the rest were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were you yourself threatened with death at all?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Once we were taken out earlier than usual and lined up to sing the anthem because one of the officers was leaving for Vukovar. All this was happening before the fall of Vukovar. Two or three days later, the news came that he had been killed in Vukovar and then we were subjected to special mistreatment in that camp. We were lined up. An execution squad was standing there prepared. They orchestrated the whole show of an execution, and we believed we would be killed. So they staged it all to make us believe that we would be executed then and there, and ultimately they let us go back into the barn. But it's something you can't forget. And they threatened us all the time that Chetniks would come and slit our throats. We had to listen to that all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were there any women detained at Begejci while you were there?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: There were around 20 women after the fall of Vukovar. I remember one of them who spent five or six days together with us in the barn. Her hands were tied, and looking at this sketch she was on the same side where this man died. Those women were later transferred to the same building that housed our guards' dormitory. Those guards were military policemen or whatever I should call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And for clarity, is that the building marked here with a 4 on the diagram?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Yes, that's building number 4. That's where those women stayed until the end, I don't know in which room exactly. We would see them around that building or outside the building, so we assumed they were there the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: What ethnicity were these women?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I was in no position to talk to them and we were not allowed to talk freely anyway, but I suppose they were from Vukovar. I suppose most of them were Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: With the usher's help, could you indicate where they were located for the first few days in the main barn, if you could use a number 5 to indicate that.

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: So this part here where that man died, the one who succumbed to the beatings, marked with green. There were around 20 of them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could I ask you to place the number 5 next to that.

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage we would tender this diagram which has been MFI'd as P1638, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to these women, are you aware of any of them being mistreated?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I didn't see anything, but I heard later that there had been rapes, that they were -- raped some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Are you aware of who carried out these rapes?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I can only suppose they were raped by men who were guarding them, by the guards, but that's only my assumption. I didn't see it. I can only tell you what I heard and what I can suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Are you aware of any of these women suffering injuries or being injured?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: The older woman had a broken arm and she was sitting there the whole time. That's how I still remember her, with her arm broken. She was a case that needed to be moved to the hospital, and even without that, the living conditions there were totally inadequate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get the photograph which is 65 ter document 6415, if that's all right, on the monitor. And I see the time, I think we should be able to deal with this quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Witness, were these the women detained at Begejci?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I cannot recognise anyone, but that's what they would have looked like. Only this person wearing something very white could be the woman with a broken arm but I cannot recognise the face. It was a long time ago, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'd tender that for admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object because the witness did not recognise anyone on the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: In light of that objection, we would simply ask to MFI for a subsequent witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That will be MFI'd, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Should be assigned Exhibit Number P1641, MFI'd. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And I see that the time is now ready for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Witness, we will take the first break now. We'll come back at 11.00. The Court usher will escort you out of court. Thank you. Just one moment, please. Just one moment. Closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, before the break, you mentioned that you had to report to the guards whenever you needed to go to the toilet. Where were the toilets?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: The toilet was to the right of the barn. And to go to the toilet you had to go out, and before that you had to report to those two guys, Mirko or Krasniqi had to know about it, and in front of the gate by the machine-gun nest there were guards armed with rifles. And at night, people going to the toilet were sometimes mistreated. They were made to sing songs or -- national anthems or sometimes they had to push their heads through the wire fence. So people were afraid of going to the toilet at night. It was important to know the words of the Yugoslav national anthem by heart because if they forced you to sing it and you didn't know the words, then you would be beaten. There were the two black men from Sri Lanka who didn't speak the language, had the words of the national anthem written to them, we wrote down the words for them so they could rehearse the words because they too had to sing the Yugoslav national anthem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, who was in charge of the Begejci camp as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I don't know, I'm not sure about his rank. I think he was a major and his last name was Zivanovic. A man by that name was mentioned at the time and he was the highest-ranking person there. I think he was a major but I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And for the avoidance of any doubt, he was a major in what army?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You also mentioned earlier that the ICRC or, sorry, the Red Cross visited on one occasion. When they visited, were they able to see all of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: When the Red Cross was expected to come to make a list of us, some ten people or so were hidden. One was said to be a sniper, but the man was so cross-eyed that it was difficult to imagine that he had been a sniper. We had to state our personal information to the Red Cross representative. There were people at various places inside that barn who would make a list of us and we gave them our personal information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for the next couple of questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Aside from the visits you've just mentioned, were there any other visits of people from outside the camp that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: There were soldiers, mostly reserve soldiers, who were keeping guard also could receive visitors during the weekend when the high-ranking officers were away. When we were let out of the barn, we saw people looking toward us and they were being told how many people any of us had killed. It felt like in a zoo, as if we were animals being shown to the visitors. It was very ugly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were there ever any TV crews present at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get a redaction there of the last reference to the relative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That will be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And, Witness, when did you eventually leave the Begejci camp approximately?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Must have been in early December, maybe on the 10th. There was an exchange to which we were taken by bus. Our belongings were returned to us then, so people were able to get some things back, and a bus took us to Bosanski Samac where we were exchanged. We also saw buses from other camps. There was some 600 of us who were exchanged for some 120 officers from Bjelovar. The exchange took place at Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we get 65 ter document 793 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, this article refers to a group of over 600 exchanged persons who had been held at Begejci, Stajicevo, and Nis arriving in Zagreb on 12th of December. Is this the same group that you were part of that was exchanged?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Yes, this could be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The article refers to a location called Kutija Sibica where they stayed for a night. What is that location? It's in the first paragraph, the last line in English.

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. Kutija Sibica is a sports hall in Zagreb where people were received. I was among them and it was at Kutija Sibica. Probably there were other places too. I spent the night in that hall. There were doctors, whoever wanted to be examined could, and there were beds in that sports hall. That's where we were received. After that, we went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And the people that were exchanged in the same group, were they civilians or soldiers or was it a mix of civilians and soldiers from the people that had been detained in the camps that were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I suppose that three-quarters of the men at Begejci were exchanged and then there were people from other camps because there was a total of 600-odd people. And the people who were with me from Begejci were civilians. There was only a group of about 20 men whom I saw wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We would seek to admit document 793.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P1642. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now get document 789. This is also a newspaper article and this should be tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And while that's coming up I'll note the article has a quote from an individual called Griesbacher or Griesbacher. Do you know who this individual is?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Griesbacher was the leader of that group of 20 soldiers belonging to the ZNG. They were from Belisce and the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And he says that they could hear the screams -- sorry, I'm just finding the quote. The screams of those being beaten by the federal soldiers. People died without treatment. You've mentioned one person dying while you were at Begejci. Are you aware of other people dying in detention?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: There was a group that went to other camps to work. Allegedly, three more camps were to be opened in the vicinity of Zrenjanin. And these people spread information about how many people killed or were killed or died. They are mentioning these beatings, but that was the normal procedure. Everybody who arrived was beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: We would seek to tender this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P1643. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, prior to you're arrest originally in Titov Vrbas that you described, were you involved in events in Suhopolje?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Upon returning from Zagreb, I was heading for Novi Sad when, around 5.00 or 5.30 a.m., a friend called me up asking me to come to a building there. Other people from Suhopolje were there and they were forming a Crisis Staff - that's what they called it - for the village. And they also invited me because an attack on relatively large barracks was being prepared. They had appeals to the personnel of the barracks to surrender and we were called in to help in the organisation. A bus was nearby. There were no weapons. I understood that to be some sort of civil protection at the time. The barracks surrendered, and later we were deployed in the streets as guards and later on we went home. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And were you armed at the -- during these events?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I didn't have any weapons. Some individuals had so-called light weapons, such as pistols or hunting rifles or make-shift rifles. I didn't see any weapons where I was. The one who relieved me as sentry was armed with a hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And were you in a uniform?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: No. I was wearing blue jeans and a leather jacket. In a word, I was in civilian clothes and everybody else was too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Final question: What impact did your detention at Begejci have on your life and what impact did it have on the life of other detainees that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: After that experience, there are probably physical consequences. I had frequent kidney inflammations because we had to lie on the concrete floor. And the mental consequences, I don't know, for many nights after the exchange I couldn't sleep, I had nightmares, but I was able to overcome that more or less. Of course, I cannot forget that experience. As regards my family life, I never consummated my first marriage and -- well, in a word, the consequence is that I haven't been the same man I was before. The most difficult thing is to describe the mental state I was in and everything I went through during my stay at that camp because I was in constant fear that I might be shot or that I might fare badly. It's very difficult to describe what you feel in such a situation. Of course whatever -- however skilful I may be or anyone may be with words, the listener can never fully appreciate what we went through.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my questions on direct examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I'm Zoran Zivanovic. I am the Defence counsel of Goran Hadzic. I'm going to ask you some questions about your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, just one moment, please. Mr. Witness, as you and Mr. Zivanovic speak the same language but it has to be interpreted so that we can understand it as well, would you please be careful not to start your answer too shortly or too quickly after the question so that there is no overlap and even a little pause between. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw in your earlier statements that you were interrogated several times after your arrest on the 5th of November and you said that, even at the beginning, the person interrogating you knew many details from your life. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Yes. If you mean the interrogation at the provincial SUP, I was surprised, to be honest. There was a man with a dark complexion and he knew many names of people from where I was and he almost knew what I was wearing at any point in time. I don't know where he got that information from.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you know that you were among the guards at Suhopolje when the barracks was taken?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: He even knew where exactly I was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me the following. You said that the number one man at Begejci, where you were taken later, was a major of the JNA by the name of Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I believe that was his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with him?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I only saw him from a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Given the mistreatment you underwent and other detainees too, did anyone contact him to tell him what was going on?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: There was no way of getting close to him. There was a procedure in place. I mentioned the two men at the exit or at the barn gate, Mirko and Krasniqi, and they were the go-betweens between us and the military police. That was the only way you could reach anybody. I never heard of anyone talking to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned Mirko and Krasniqi, were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: No, no. They had the same treatment as the rest of us. We were all camp inmates. They were dressed the same as the rest of us. They were chosen, probably, among all those people to be intermediaries of sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean like room monitors but they were basically also detainees?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Yes, they were camp inmates who I heard had been beaten something horrible when they first arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you something. You connected the beatings with the interrogations that followed?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it normal procedure for a prisoner to be beaten first and then taken to some sort of interrogation?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I told you already the whole story about myself, but all the camp inmates went through the same. When they arrived, they would be beaten at the entrance to the barn. The rest of us were lying down, covered over the head with blankets, and we would have to stay that way until they finished. Then the new person would be given a place in the barn. A few days later they would be called out and beaten again, and then they would be called out to be taken outside of the barn to be questioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And who did the beatings?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Only those who were allowed to go into the barn. There were just a few of them. I told you their nicknames or what they called each other, Zare, Borko, Vojo, Rambo. There was one man whom they called Sergeant. About seven or eight of them. They were designated persons who came in. There were other reservists, older men, who were standing guard at certain points behind the wire fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now you've enumerated all these names. Can you tell me, were they wearing some uniforms or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: They were in JNA uniforms. From the start in Paragovo, all of them were military policemen with the distinctive white belts, which they didn't wear all the time, but they had those white belts which are a distinctive mark of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me about the interrogations. Were they conducted again by military policemen with those white belts or by men who were dressed differently?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: That depends on the stage of interrogation. In Paragovo they were officers who interrogated us. There was a major and a captain, I believe. Later there was a sergeant with that bottle of brandy who I mentioned, but I'm not sure about this point because this was a weekend so I'm not sure it was official. But after that the incident when six of them beat them, I went through the regular routine; that is to say, I was brought by the military policemen, I passed by their dormitory, and then among some heaps of hay, I received a piece of paper on which I was supposed to write my fifth or sixth statement. Then I was beaten by military policemen who said I hadn't written enough. There were mice running all around me. While I was writing, a mouse skipped across the desk, so you can imagine the environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's clear one thing up. So in Paragovo you were questioned by JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in Begejci later, those were military policemen?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Yes, military policemen. I was taken out later for the verification of my written statement, but it was done in the way I described. I was alone in that room where I wrote that so-called statement, and then I was summoned by an officer to explain my statement. They were probably comparing that statement with the previous ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember that officer whom you were brought for the purpose of checking your statement? Did he have a white belt like the military police or did he have a normal officer uniform?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I can't remember the one who was in Begejci. He was certainly in uniform, but I cannot remember his face anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember his rank?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: There were mainly captains, majors. In Paragovo and in the other place, there were no warrant officers or other NCOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, just a moment. That time when you were taken for your statement to be checked, apart from you and that officer, was there anyone else?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: They were always in twos. They came and went. That had no special significance. They just wanted to check the statement. I did not get any bad treatment on that occasion, I wasn't beaten. That's not what I remember it for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps complain to that officer about the treatment you had?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: It was not possible to complain because there had been statements by camp inmates referring to the Geneva Conventions and the answer was -- you can imagine. We were treated there like dogs. You felt like you were less than nothing. There was no question of complaining or even saying anything. You could only get even worse things coming, more

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Should we get a redaction? I'm not sure how many relatives of inmates visited at the time so I'm trying to be stuck to that line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask you one more thing. If I understood you correctly, you were afraid to complain to that officer because then things would have gotten even worse for you?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: Right. I mean, everybody got the same treatment. Everybody was afraid to say anything. There was no point in it. Because you were simply unable to understand why any of that was happening at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that in your previous answer you mentioned that there were some people who had invoked Geneva Conventions. I wonder where did they invoke the conventions, with the officers who interrogated them or with military policemen?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: In my hearing they mentioned it to military policemen and, of course, the answer was very coarse, very rude, explaining in no uncertain terms what the military policemen thought about Geneva Conventions. So these people never dared to mention it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And none of them mentioned it later to those officers?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: We could not get access to these officers except through the military policemen or those two men, Krasniqi and the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And during the verification of your statements and during questioning, I suppose at least their statements were also verified?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: People were beaten, at least that's what I heard when they came back, and there were even people who fainted from fear the moment their names were called out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I understood that part, but did any of those who were invited, like you were, to verify their statement before JNA officers, did any one of them complain to the JNA officers and invoke Geneva Conventions there?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think so, and in any case there was no point because no one was interested. If they had any intention to improve our living conditions, they could have. Instead, it was what it was. At one point we were all -- we all had our heads shaven because somebody got lice, and if we got one single bath just before the exchange, you can imagine. They were aware of all that. There were no basic living conditions, there was no food.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Thank you, Your Honours. I am done. I just finished my cross-examination, but it is not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, in your last answer you were describing how the detainees had their heads shaven and the living conditions and lack of food and you said: "They were aware of all that." Who do you mean when you say "they were aware of all that"?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: I mean the superior officers of the JNA who were in command there practically. They were able to order for something to be changed or not. They saw the living conditions and I said this in answer to this question about why we didn't complain to the officers invoking Geneva Conventions. That was my answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: No further questions on re-direct. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, I have a little question to clear something up, I mean something on the transcript page 37, lines 18 through 25. You were talking about the crisis committee in Suhopolje before your arrest in Titov Vrbas. I did not understand what this crisis committee or Crisis Staff was all about. Was it a little one made up of a few persons or was it a large assembly with a great number of participants?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: They were residents, local residents, of Suhopolje. My former schoolmates, people with whom I had grown up. They organised themselves. It was like any other Crisis Staff that is normally organised in case of a natural disaster, in an effort to deal with the problems. In this case, they had organised themselves to defend themselves in case something happened, and in this case they were also afraid of what might happen if the army left the barracks and went away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what was the role of this Crisis Staff? Was it to stop the army from leaving the barracks or to fight against outside assailants?

utterances.speaker: GH-071
utterances.text: If I understand anything, they were not really able to put up any defence or to stop the army because they had no weapons, nothing. They just organised themselves because it was done everywhere. There was also something called civilian protection and they organised themselves in the same way. That's the way I understand it. I wasn't living there at the time, but when I happened to be there, I was invited by friends and I worked together with them at that moment, while I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I understand better now. This is enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, this brings an end to your testimony. We thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness. We wish you a safe journey home. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you very much. Closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll try to be as brief as possible. The next witness testified previously in a different case and the Defence had asked or was asking if there was a B/C/S transcript of his prior ICTY testimony and there is not. Those are not made by the Tribunal, they -- it's possible they exist for other reasons but not for this witness. The -- what's normally done in these situations is the audio -- the audiotape of the prior testimony in B/C/S can serve as the B/C/S version, although the practice has been that we have not been disclosing those to the Defence as a matter of course. They're available to all parties from the Registry. But in any event, we don't have the B/C/S audio of the witness's prior testimony, and the Defence, it's my understanding, has -- would like to have some possibility for the accused to review that prior testimony before the witness testifies. And we had never obtained that previously from the Registry. I think the Defence also had never obtained that previously. And so the suggestion - and obviously subject to what my learned friend might say - we've been in touch during the breaks today and with Registry and we think we can have the audio portion available from Registry this afternoon. It has to be processed and it could then be made available to the Defence to enable the accused, Mr. Hadzic, to at least hear the prior testimony and consult with counsel before the witness testifies. The witness is down for just one hour of direct examination. As I indicated in earlier -- in an e-mail to the Chamber, we've -- we had the possibility of coming up short this week because the next witness has to absolutely positively testify within the given time-frame. So I think there's ample time. So the suggestion would be to break for the rest of today, to obtain the audio B/C/S version, make it available to the Defence, which would give the accused some time to review that before the examination begins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Anything from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Our position would be that under 66(A)(ii), Mr. Hadzic is entitled to the prior statements of the witness, and we say that that's -- that is satisfied in respect of prior statements that are not Rule 92 ter if it's just the audio. When it is a 92 ter statement, consultation with the client is, of course, made very difficult if we're working from a long series of transcripts and trying to compare that with an audiotape. So, first of all, we would just like to make a standing request at this point that somehow the resources of the Tribunal be deployed so that if a 92 ter statement is being submitted in the form of transcripts of prior testimony, that we also have a B/C/S version of those transcripts. There are other cases in which transcripts have been generated, possibly by outside agencies, but they are on the ICTY web site. So I understand it's not beyond the capacity of the Tribunal to do that. Now, what occurred in this case and what has happened in previous cases - and there have only been, I think, about two witnesses prior to this where the 92 ter statement was in the form of prior testimony, and we on the Defence noticed that that was the case and requested an audiotape or an audio of the testimony and provided it to Mr. Hadzic for consultation. In this case, we didn't notice until too late that we hadn't received that disclosure of the prior testimony of the witness. And so we would now say that -- and even though we haven't done it in the past, we do believe there's an obligation for the Prosecution to give that to us, the audiotape, of any prior testimony of the witness, particularly when it's going to be tendered as a 92 ter statement. And on that basis, we would at least request that the witness be delayed until tomorrow so that Mr. Hadzic has the opportunity to review that audiotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just to make sure that we understand correctly. The statement -- the testimony we are speaking about right now, is that the 92 ter statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's testimony from an earlier ICTY case. If I could just make a couple additional comments --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- in response. As counsel's indicated, there are two prior witnesses for whom a transcript was the 92 ter statement. And, first of all, it's never been suggested previously that there is a disclosure obligation for the Prosecution to provide and to -- what will essentially be an obligation to make a transcript in B/C/S where one doesn't already exist. This is new. We've talked over the break about trying to see if we can, first of all, identify the number of additional witnesses to come for whom this might be an issue and to see who they are, to see what we can do about that. I think if the Prosecution undertook to assist in producing B/C/S transcripts of English versions of ICTY transcripts, it's something that we would do voluntarily not as something that is an obligation. Both of the parties in this case have access to the audiotapes of all witnesses' prior testimonies in the related cases to this one. So there's nothing uneven about access. CLSS, the people who do translations, generally I'm quite confident their position certainly has consistently in my experience been that they don't do transcripts, they do translations.
