Here we're just talking about having someone listen to the audio in B/C/S and to write down in B/C/S a transcript of that; CLSS won't do that. So I guess my observations are, number one, it's not a disclosure obligation that can be attributed to the Prosecution. Having said that, we can look and see who the remaining witnesses are and whether OTP staff, because ultimately it will be OTP language staff, the people who sit in the proofing sessions, et cetera, who would be asked to make the transcript for the Defence. And I'm open to a discussion along those lines, but that's for the witnesses to come. So those are my -- I guess my remarks in response. We don't see it as a disclosure obligation. The transcripts from the Seselj case do exist in B/C/S. I think that was an order that was issued specifically to that case because there was a self-represented accused in that case. In addition, as counsel's mentioned, there are some NGOs, some bodies, outside of the Tribunal that have undertaken to produce B/C/S transcripts of ICTY proceedings, but it's really hit-or-miss as to whether they've selected a witness who might actually be a witness in this case. So -- but in any event that's perhaps for future just the point being that we don't believe that -- and we would resist and I guess oppose the Defence request or suggestion that there's a disclosure obligation to require the Prosecution to generate B/C/S transcripts of ICTY testimony. There's no disclosure violation. I don't think that's being suggested. But the witness's prior evidence, the statement in English, has gone across a long time ago. They missed it. We weren't aware it was a problem because it's not been raised in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As a matter of curiosity, have there been -- when these transcripts are produced externally, have issues of authenticity arisen which have had to be resolved?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We have not tendered any of those outside transcripts into evidence as Rule 92 ter statement in this case. There is one witness who I can think of for whom this was done, that is to say, an outside body made a B/C/S transcript of his prior ICTY evidence that's been disclosed to the Defence. If we have that, we would obviously disclose it, but we don't go looking for those to outside bodies to see who might have made a transcript of a Prosecution witness. Again, that's a source that is -- those are being made to make that available to the public. And so anybody can go get those transcripts. So we haven't used those and would not tender one of those as a 92 ter statement in this case, which -- and along the same lines, should the OTP make a B/C/S transcript of one of these in a spirit of co-operation with the Defence for any subsequent witnesses who are yet to come, because it's an OTP transcript made by a language assistant and it's not going to be an official Tribunal transcript, that we would necessarily -- would be looking to label as an official transcript. That's only coming from CLSS. And as I said, I don't think they do those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If I may very briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If I may very briefly, Mr. President, just to clarify the situation. We have neither the audio nor a transcript in respect of this particular 92 ter statement and that's really the core of the problem that we're dealing with right now. Going forward -- and if any of my remarks were interpreted as an allegation of misconduct or reproach, that was not the intention. We are in somewhat of a grey area, but nonetheless, we say that under 66(A)(ii), that obligation does rest on the Prosecution to provide prior statements of the witnesses and we believe there is jurisprudence that says that that must be provided in the language of the accused. Now, that may be satisfied by audio, Mr. President, and ultimately that may be the position taken by the Chamber, but you may understand how difficult it is to work with a very long, lengthy audio, without time marks in relation to a long transcript. It does make that work difficult and there is also the issue of translation. But what we're primarily concerned with is being able to be on the same page, so to speak, in English and in the language of the accused. So we would, indeed, be requesting that both a transcript and the audio be provided in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: For the moment we will have to decide on the problem for the next witness, and I do agree that the best thing to do is to adjourn for the day and to give the Defence the opportunity to listen to the audio which will be provided by the Prosecutor. Am I -- is that a good understanding of what you were saying, Mr. Stringer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the Prosecution, our case manager, has already been in touch with Registry. There's been some consultation with the Registry personnel already, and we're told that the audio can be provided to the Prosecution this afternoon. There may be an additional logistical issue that might even perhaps require the Chamber's involvement in terms of providing the disk to the accused at the Detention Unit because there are some procedures that come into play on those -- on that issue. But I think that -- my guess is that Registry should be able to look after that. Once we've provided -- once we have the disk and have it ready, there's -- I think the Prosecution's not in a position to ensure that it actually goes to the UNDU.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But I suppose that with the help of the Registry that would work? Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, the Registrar tells me that you should then provide the disk before 4.00. Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Assuming we can obtain it from Registry, we will give it to Registry before 4.00. There is some technical processing that has to happen apparently before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I will not try to understand that, Mr. Stringer. The issue about how to deal with this in the future, I think we need a little bit of time to think that one over and we might even ask for written submissions on that matter, but if so, we will let you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: On that point, it -- today we're going to look to see whether -- how many remaining 92 ter witnesses are those for whom a transcript is their statement, I think it's not many, and it may be that working with the Defence we can find an arrangement that would -- if they're satisfied with what we're able to produce, we might have enough time to make that happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If that is all, court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 2nd day of May, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.07 p.m.,
